attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. He presents the stagnation as a fact that others are covering up.

semantics.note: The draft keeps both parts: little capability gain over the past year, and diminishing returns overall. Dropping 'really' does not change what he committed to. The claim about investors' and the media's conduct is rightly left out.

contract.note: He named no measure. Reading this as 'frontier capability improved little from April 2024 to April 2025' is the ordinary reading. The contract notes the gap between benchmarks and everyday usefulness. Letting a clear contradiction of the little-progress part contradict the whole assertion is reasonable.

evidence.note: METR preprint dated before the post (March 2025). It compares historical models on the same task suites. The length of tasks models can complete doubled roughly every six months, and every three months for 2024-only models. That is substantial progress with no sign of slowing. It does not measure returns per dollar.

reviews.rationale: An independent evaluation from before publication shows large gains over the year on fixed software and reasoning tasks, so the claim of little progress fails. The trend did not slow either, which undercuts the 'slowing gains' sense of diminishing returns. Returns per dollar are not measured, but the contract treats the capability contradiction as enough to decide the claim.

attribution.note: His own first-person forecast ('I expect') in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I expect' is unqualified expectation, so this is a scored forecast. 'The latter cost' correctly refers to the roughly $1bn spent on infrastructure OpenAI owns. No deadline and no size threshold were given.

contract.note: It uses the ~$1bn owned-infrastructure figure as the baseline and reads 'balloon' as a substantial increase, without inventing a deadline. Requiring owned costs to be kept separate from leases and equity stakes matches his wording.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own January 2026 announcement. It describes a $500M equity stake in SB Energy and a data-center lease. Neither is an owned-infrastructure cost figure, so it cannot support the forecast.
Company statement that Stargate I in Abilene is partly running (built by Oracle). It gives no figure for OpenAI's owned-infrastructure spending.

reviews.rationale: This is a forecast with no deadline. Neither the support condition nor the early-resolution rule is met: no spending series separates owned infrastructure from leases or equity, and none ties a substantial increase to Stargate. Stargate also has not been completed or terminated. The evidence does not settle it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own analytical sentence. The Altman posts he cites are quoted, but the inference that OpenAI has capacity problems is his.

semantics.note: 'Suggests' marks an inference he endorses, not a probability hedge like 'may' or 'likely'. The core claim is that OpenAI had significant capacity issues. The 'unclear' clause states his uncertainty and is correctly left unscored.

contract.note: It scores the checkable core, capacity-driven limits and delays from late February to the post date, and sets the 'unclear' clause aside. That reading is fair and ordinary and narrows the broad 'any mention' to his actual context.

evidence.note: Reputable report: in the period, Altman said capacity challenges would cause delays, breakage and slow service.
Same report: OpenAI held back the free image-tool launch and disabled Sora video for new users to ease capacity.
7 April 2025 report: Altman gave capacity as one reason for delaying GPT-5.
March 2025 CoreWeave deal expanding OpenAI's capacity. It bears only on the unscored 'unclear' clause and does not refute the capacity problems.

reviews.rationale: Reports from the period quote OpenAI's CEO linking rate limits, delays and slow service to capacity shortages, and describe features restricted for capacity reasons. That meets the support condition. The CoreWeave deal concerns only the unscored 'unclear' clause.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Cannot reduce its costs at this point' captures the asserted inability. The causal 'because' clause about plentiful money is background. Whether 'make things cheaper' means total spending or cost per unit is not specified.

contract.note: Reading it as OpenAI's ability to cut its own operating costs is ordinary. The contract rightly separates prices from internal costs and flags total versus per-unit costs. Using January–March 2025 for 'at this point' is a reasonable choice for an undated present-tense claim.

evidence.note: OpenAI's January 2025 claim that o3-mini is cost-efficient. A company statement about itself with no internal cost figures, so it cannot establish whether OpenAI's own costs fell.

OpenAI's publication-day statement that inference efficiency gains allowed lower GPT-4.1 prices. It hints that per-unit savings were possible but gives no internal cost data and falls outside the target quarter.

reviews.rationale: Both items are OpenAI's own efficiency and pricing statements. Under the contract, prices cannot establish internal costs, and no comparable operating-cost figures for the quarter are in the packet. The efficiency claims cast some doubt on the claim but do not settle it either way.
